Revised assessment: The FOMC appropriately notes that the coronavirus will weigh on near-term activity and increase downside risks, but its rapid move to the 0–1/4 percent range, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, and expanded repo and dollar swap lines are consistent with the credit-channel and financial-accelerator literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist), which shows that easing financial frictions can stabilize aggregate demand and the flow of credit. With market-based inflation compensation falling yet survey-based long-run expectations little changed, an inflation-forecast-targeting perspective (Svensson; Svensson and Woodford) and the Taylor-principle logic support aggressive easing at the effective lower bound in a potential liquidity-trap environment. Given muted inflation pressures and anchored expectations, these policies should cushion—but not fully offset—the contraction, supporting the Fed’s maximum employment and price stability objectives as conditions normalize.
